item.title: Does Child Sexual Abuse Ruin Women for Partner Sex for Life?
item.description:
Sex

Does Child Sexual Abuse Ruin Women for Partner Sex for Life?

Most survivors can experience happy partner sex—if they use one specific therapy.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • The myth is that survivors of child sexual abuse are often sexually impaired for life.
  • That's possible, but a recent study shows that it's possible to heal and experience enjoying partner sex.
  • The key is to reintroduce survivors to their bodies' ability to experience pleasure.

The conventional wisdom declares that child sex abuse (CSA) is so horrendous, so traumatic, so psychologically devastating that survivors, overwhelmingly women, develop long-term post-traumatic stress disorder and deep fears of partner sex, often avoiding it for years, sometimes for the rest of their lives. If CSA survivors manage to return to sex, the conventional wisdom holds that they do it just for their partners, don’t enjoy it, and suffer sex problems—difficulty becoming aroused and working up to orgasms.

CSA is, indeed, deeply traumatic, and may involve long-term sexual impairment. But a recent study shows that as CSA survivors leave childhood and become young adult women, many are able to enjoy partner sex—if they explore who they are sexually by embracing self-sexing.

The Study

University of Nebraska researchers surveyed 77 young adult women CSA survivors, average age 20, asking, among other issues, if they intentionally avoided partner sex. Some of the women had real problems with sex. But contrary to the conventional wisdom, the researchers found that if the women self-sexed regularly, CSA did not result in long-term sexual avoidance or high risk of sex problems. With regular solo sex, the women generally stopped avoiding partner sex and were less likely to suffer sex problems.

Healing Is Possible

Of course, immediately after people experience any significant trauma, they are quite likely to avoid the activity that produced it. But in the equestrian realm, there’s an old saying: “Get back up on the horse that threw you.” After riders get thrown off horses, riding instructors urge them to confront their fears and ride again.

Compared with getting thrown from horses, CSA is more fraught and more psychologically complex, but this study suggests that the riding advice still holds. Sexual trauma survivors may not be able to escape memories of what happened to them. But they are not doomed to a life without lovemaking. They can recover—that is, experience enjoyable, problem-free partner sex—if they explore their sexuality at a pace that feels comfortable for them, and include regular solo sex in the process.

Staci Haines is the author of Healing Sex: A Mind-Body Approach to Healing Sexual Trauma. She is also a CSA survivor. After years of struggling with her own recovery, she now enjoys a pleasurable, fulfilling sex life and has become a psychotherapist specializing in helping abuse survivors rediscover erotic pleasure.

“Healing is possible,” she explains, “emotional and sexual healing. I tell survivors: You survived. You’re more powerful than what happened to you. Victimization is terrible. Surviving it is very hard. So is recovery. But now that you’re an adult, you have the capacity to recover and to build the life—and the sex life—you choose.”

article continues after advertisement

How? Haines practices somatic therapy, which employs physical touch to reintroduce survivors to their bodies’ ability to experience pleasure. Those somatic explorations must feel safe. They begin with gentle, patient, self-massage all over, and eventually proceed to self-sexing.

Haines’ approach dovetails with the findings of the recent study. Compared with the women who did not engage in regular solo sex, those who did were significantly less likely to shun sex, and more likely to experience pleasurable partner lovemaking.

Unfortunately, self-sexing remains culturally stigmatized, and for many, a source of shame. The shame often stems from the Judeo-Christian religious tradition, which emphasizes the Bible’s first commandment to human beings: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). As a result, many religious Jews and Christians—Muslims, too—abhor solo sex, declaring that God approves only of heterosexual marital sex with the clear intention of procreation. While many people sometimes engage in sex to have children, many others view sex as a path to pleasure. Around the world, the most popular type of sex is the solo variety.

Self-sexing is not just pleasurable. It’s also therapeutic. It’s fundamental to the treatment of premature ejaculation in men, and women’s difficulties working up to orgasms. The study provides evidence that self-sexing is also therapeutic for CSA (and I bet for post-childhood sexual trauma as well).

Get Professional Help

In one way, the conventional wisdom is correct. CSA and other sexual traumas cause deep psychological damage. Recovery is possible, but it takes time—and usually professional help. Survivors might begin by reading Haine’s book and then working with a trauma-informed psychotherapist, ideally one whose approach incorporates somatic therapy and regular self-massage that includes solo sex.

item.title: AI Is Here: What Therapists Can Do Now
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Is Here: What Therapists Can Do Now

Five ways to help clients use AI thoughtfully while preserving human connection.

Posted October 6, 2026

Key points
  • AI is already part of many clients' support systems, so therapists benefit from learning to work with it.
  • Approach clients' AI use with curiosity, not judgment, so they keep talking about it openly.
  • Chatbots can inform, but empathy, attunement, and trust are what make human therapy heal.
  • Clear boundaries and honest talk about privacy help clients use AI and therapy together.

As a therapist, I have noticed a growing number of clients using artificial intelligence (AI) before reaching out to a licensed psychotherapist. This trend — where an AI chatbot may be the first place humans ask questions about anxiety, relationships, trauma, depression, or other emotional concerns — is growing.

A 2026 study published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% of adolescents and young adults surveyed in 2025 had used an AI chatbot for mental health advice, compared with 13.1% in 2024. Among those who used chatbots for mental health advice, most described the experience as at least somewhat helpful.

When I first noticed this trend in my practice, I felt uneasy. How accurate is the information clients receive? What about privacy and safety? And could AI eventually replace therapists?

From Unease to Acceptance

Over time, I realized I needed a different approach: acceptance. AI is here to stay. Rather than viewing it only as a dubious threat, therapists may need to learn how to work with clients who are using it.

AI is increasingly becoming part of clients' emotional and informational support systems. Some enter therapy after asking a chatbot about symptoms, relationships, coping strategies, or possible diagnoses. In that sense, they are bringing a new, nonhuman part of their support network into therapy.

What AI Can't Replace

I do not believe that AI can currently replace the human therapeutic relationship. Information alone is rarely enough to heal emotional wounds. Psychotherapy with a human offers something different: empathy, attunement, trust, presence, relational repair, and the experience of being understood by another person.

At the same time, AI can have value. Chatbots can provide accessible information, help clients organize their thoughts, and introduce psychological concepts. Used thoughtfully, AI may augment psychotherapy rather than replace it.

The question for me is no longer, "Will AI replace therapists?" It is, "How can therapists help clients use AI thoughtfully while preserving what is uniquely human about psychotherapy?"

1. Get Curious About Their AI Use

I begin with curiosity. What are they asking the chatbot? What advice have they received? What has been helpful, confusing, or incomplete?

article continues after advertisement

Their use of AI may reflect a need for reassurance, information, validation, or immediate support. Understanding how they use AI can also help me better understand what they are seeking emotionally.

2. Stay Nonjudgmental

Therapists should approach clients' AI use with curiosity rather than criticism.

Clients may turn to chatbots because they want information, feel uncomfortable asking another person, or are trying to manage distress. If they feel judged, they may stop discussing their AI use or disengage from therapy.

We do not have to agree with everything AI tells a client in order to remain curious about why the information matters to them.

3. Name the Disagreements Openly

I am honest with clients that my clinical perspective may sometimes differ from what a chatbot has suggested.

Rather than treating this as a competition between therapist and AI, we can examine the information together. Does it fit the client's circumstances? Is important context missing? Is general information being interpreted as personalized clinical advice?

Ultimately, neither the therapist nor AI should make decisions for the client. Our role is to help clients think clearly and make informed choices.

4. Compare What Therapy and AI Each Offer

Human psychotherapy provides empathy, presence, emotional attunement, eye contact, and the ability to notice subtle changes in emotions, mood, behavior, and tone. It also offers an ongoing relationship in which trust, vulnerability, challenge, and repair can develop over time.

AI offers different advantages. It can provide information quickly, explain psychological concepts, and help clients generate questions and ideas.

Clients should also understand that the confidentiality protections associated with psychotherapy may not apply in the same way to information entered into AI platforms.

5. Set Clear Boundaries

In my practice, I welcome clients to discuss information they have received from AI, but I ask them not to use chatbots during therapy sessions.

I also generally discourage clients from sending me lengthy AI transcripts or reports. Instead, I ask them to verbalize what stood out in their own words: How did they understand what AI said to them? What affected them? What did they agree or disagree with?

article continues after advertisement

My therapeutic relationship is not with the chatbot. It is with the client and their experience of what the chatbot told them.

Information Isn't the Same as Change

AI will likely become increasingly integrated into how people seek mental health information. Therapists will need to continue thinking about accuracy, privacy, safety, and appropriate boundaries.

But AI may also remind us of something fundamental: People do not come to therapy only because they lack information.

A person may already know that a relationship is unhealthy, that childhood experiences continue to affect them, or that they need stronger boundaries. Knowing something intellectually does not necessarily make emotional change easier.

Psychotherapy provides a relationship in which those patterns can be understood, experienced, challenged, and gradually changed.

AI may become a useful companion in that process. But the heart of psychotherapy remains relational.

Perhaps the task ahead is not to defend therapy from AI, but to become clearer about what each can offer and to help clients use both thoughtfully.
